pains.t: Cost is the top reason food delivery users decide not to order at all.
pains.w: In a 13,000+ user survey across APAC and EU, money concerns were the single most common barrier (44%) — ordering is perceived as a more expensive way to get food than cooking or eating out, so price-sensitive users opt out before they even browse.

pains.t: New food delivery users are gated by location and sign-up before they can explore.
pains.w: New users arrive curious to browse, but the app asks for a location and pushes sign-up/sign-in before showing value, and the first screen can feel overwhelming. Evidence on the location step is mixed - some users dislike being forced to set it before exploring, while others find location reasonable for a food app and instead object to the sign-up wall that follows (the unclear "Skip"/"X" is the real friction). The shared frustration is being blocked from exploring first.

pains.t: Discovery shuts out food delivery users who are expats or have accessibility needs.
pains.w: Expat and accessibility (A11Y) users struggled to browse and get started: A11Y users find the app isn't perceived as accessible and can churn when the menu feels overwhelming, while expats hit language gaps — inconsistent translations (especially in menus and swimlanes) act as a churn driver even before install.

pains.t: Savings are hard to see — deals, Pro and loyalty don't make their value obvious to food delivery users.
pains.w: Incentives are scattered with no single entry point and low visibility, so users scroll to hunt for deals, and promised new-user discounts don't always activate after sign-up. The subscription and loyalty story is just as murky: about 1 in 5 users never subscribe to Pro despite ordering enough to break even, ~53% of subscribers churn over low perceived value, and Pro prompts can appear even to ineligible users — while competitors' loyalty programs feel clearer and stronger.

quote.text: It looks complicated. There's no united UI... the banners are separated, so I have to look one by one.

delights.t: A straightforward sign-up gets new food delivery users moving quickly.
delights.w: New users called registration easy and it helped them get to their first order without friction.

delights.t: Seeing popular restaurants up front helps new and indecisive food delivery users start.
delights.w: Popular-restaurant and social-proof recommendations gave new and less-decisive users an easy way in, matching what indecisive users lean on to choose.

jtbd.functional: Get a meal with the least effort, time, and cost.
jtbd.emotional: Satisfy a craving or treat myself.
jtbd.social: Order for — or with — other people.

pains.t: Discovery tools don't help food delivery users find or narrow to what they want.
pains.w: Two-thirds of users (66%) open the app with a dish or cuisine in mind, but search is restaurant-centric and returns the wrong things (drinks for "pizza", non-Indian for "Indian"; vendors that don't carry the dish), misleading vendor images create false expectations, and filters are hard to find and awkward (long cuisine lists, distrusted dietary filters, low usage). Empty and pre-search screens dead-end instead of guiding, so users abandon.

quote.text: I searched for Indian and here is everything but indian. 4-5 restaurants before 2 indian options come up.

pains.t: Food delivery users can't compare options side by side — and real price stays hidden until they open a menu.
pains.w: Comparing the same dish across vendors on price, deals and quality is a strong unmet need; today it means backing out and re-entering each store (web users even open one browser tab per restaurant to compare). The price ($) signal doesn't show actual price or minimum order value, so users still bounce after opening a vendor.

quote.text: I couldn't do comparison across shops, and it would be helpful to compare products across shops for prices, packaging, details.

pains.t: Faced with too many options, indecisive food delivery users fall back on a familiar place — or don't order.
pains.w: Roughly a third of users open the app without a firm choice; facing choice overload and not-always-relevant recommendations, indecisive users default to a "safe" familiar restaurant even when they wanted to explore, and some abandon the order entirely.

pains.t: Deals are confusing — food delivery users can't tell what applies or how much they'll actually save.
pains.w: Multiple overlapping incentives and unclear terms create overload, so users misjudge the real discount; the discount bar is easy to miss on the menu and voucher visibility/comprehension is low on both the vendor tile and menu, and accessing relevant promotions is high-importance, low-satisfaction.

delights.t: Food delivery users value being able to filter for free delivery.
delights.w: Every participant welcomed a free-delivery filter even when they didn't always need it — it maps directly to the budget-and-benefits lens users apply when deciding, and delivery fee is among the information they weigh most.

delights.t: A relevant deal helps food delivery users decide — and feels genuinely rewarding.
delights.w: Discounts help less-decisive users commit to a choice, and a good, applicable deal lifts how users feel about the order — especially where prices feel high, a discount makes the purchase feel worth it.

quote.text: The discount is a plus point, but having the discounts is really uplifting.

delights.t: Reordering a usual is a fast, low-effort way for food delivery users to get a familiar meal.
delights.w: Past orders and favourite restaurants are a trusted, low-effort starting point — decisive users lean on reorder to get straight to a known, safe choice without browsing.

jtbd.functional: Find something I'll enjoy fast — matching my craving, my budget, and worth the money — without opening every restaurant.
jtbd.emotional: Decide with confidence and avoid the frustration of a disappointing order.
jtbd.social: Use other people's ratings and reviews to trust a place I haven't tried.

jtbd.functional: Pay quickly and correctly, with the payment method I trust and the right voucher applied.
jtbd.emotional: Feel confident the price is final and fair — no surprises between cart and checkout.
jtbd.social: Get an order for the household over the line without hassle.

pains.t: Payment failures interrupt checkout for food delivery users.
pains.w: Payment and checkout failures disrupt ordering: SEQ analysis shows checkout is harder for new users (more steps), with the top complaints being technical/app-performance errors, payment-method problems (~18%) and voucher application - a first-time failure that can cost a new user's trust and retention.

pains.t: Vouchers that looked available get rejected at checkout — and applying the right one is too much work.
pains.w: Incentive amounts aren't consistent across the journey - the vast majority of users (10/11) are frustrated by a price difference between cart and checkout - and vouchers users expected are flagged expired, invalid or inapplicable at the cart. Users also want vouchers available at checkout, and (especially in TR) ask for automatic "soft" application rather than hunting for and applying the best deal manually - making the cart the most common abandonment point in the incentives journey.

pains.t: Getting back to a past order is slower than it should be for food delivery users.
pains.w: Reorder is a top use case, but past orders are buried beneath promotions and other elements, swimlanes often don't surface the restaurants users expect, and there's no fast track from entry to checkout — so a journey that should be one tap takes several.

delights.t: Google/Apple Pay gives food delivery users a fast, trusted way to pay.
delights.w: New users called out Google Pay / Apple Pay as a welcome, trusted checkout option — for some it's the very reason they use the app over the web.

delights.t: Cart and checkout feel easy and low-anxiety for food delivery users.
delights.w: The split between cart (review/manage) and checkout (finalise price and payment) matches users' mental model and reduces cognitive load, and recent additions like saved carts and pre-order confirmation are noticed and appreciated - overall users find the flow easy.

jtbd.functional: Know where my order is and a reliable time it will arrive.
jtbd.emotional: Feel reassured it's handled, and know I can get help fast if it isn't.
jtbd.social: Plan around the arrival so I'm ready when the food reaches me and others.

pains.t: Unreliable, jumping ETAs erode food delivery users' trust — and push them to competitors.
pains.w: About 25% of orders run late (an estimated €25M GMV lost as users cancel over delays), and inaccurate, jumping or stagnant ETAs are the single biggest driver of the CSAT gap versus competitors for both Food and QC. When the promised time slips with no clear reason, users switch to a faster rival for the same restaurant.

quote.text: I compare the ETA with Trendyol and leave Yemek... Yemeksepeti delivers in 45-60 mins, Trendyol in 15.

pains.t: Order status and real-time updates are unclear, so food delivery users are left guessing.
pains.w: Unclear or wrong order-status information is the #1 reason users contact support (~1.7M contacts a year), and Pandora lags competitors on "clear, accurate, live updates" (-12.4%) and "knowing the rider location in real-time" (-10%), leaving a 58% CSAT gap on restaurant orders. Proactive, accurate communication is what users say makes a platform feel reliable.

jtbd.functional: Get my order, on time and in good condition — or a fast, fair resolution if not.
jtbd.emotional: Feel looked after at the door, and taken care of when something goes wrong.
jtbd.social: Have a good handover moment with the rider and share the meal I ordered.

pains.t: Food quality on arrival is a recurring letdown for food delivery users.
pains.w: Returning customers cited food-quality issues on delivered orders as a repeat frustration at the receiving moment.

pains.t: When an order is cancelled, food delivery users are left with a poor recovery path.
pains.w: Cancellations are large-scale (~2.6% of orders, ~22M a year, ~€226M GMV lost), driven by delays, accidental orders, item unavailability and rider unavailability, plus ~2M users needing to modify an order after placing it. The cancellation screens do little to help users recover (reorder or explore) and refund communication is weak, damaging confidence in the platform.

pains.t: Getting help when something goes wrong is slow and can't capture the real problem.
pains.w: Support and issue resolution rate ~12% below competitors — the biggest experience gap — and help-center forms don't cover the nuance of a case (e.g. a missing item inside a set meal), pushing users to hunt for a live agent. Volumes are huge (650k+ subscribers alone contacted support in a single month), and a poor support experience measurably reduces how often people order.

quote.text: There's no breakdown of the set, so I can't actually choose the item that's missing.

delights.t: A good rider handover creates a real emotional connection for food delivery users.
delights.w: The human moment at the door is a genuine bright spot — users form positive connections with riders, and most actively want an after-delivery way to thank or tip them, which reinforces the goodwill and their intent to reorder.

pains.t: New QC users are gated by location and sign-up before they can explore.
pains.w: The shared app onboarding asks for a location and pushes sign-up before showing value, and the first screen feels overwhelming - friction for newcomers arriving for groceries. Evidence on location is mixed (some accept it as normal; others resent the sign-up wall that follows); the common frustration is being blocked from exploring first.

pains.t: QC users perceive Pandora groceries as more expensive than shopping in person.
pains.w: Affordability is the critical barrier: it blocks ~40% of new users and drives ~36% of existing users to competitors - driven by perceived high product prices and fees more than a lack of promotions - so lower prices are the single most effective acquisition trigger (62%). For recurring restock, users prefer large online supermarkets for range and pricing. Value is also hard to judge overall: Pro's savings and loyalty rewards feel unclear (many who'd break even never subscribe), and competitors' loyalty programs feel stronger.

pains.t: Pandora's grocery offer is easy to miss and hard to trust for produce you can't see.
pains.w: New-to-QC users assume search is for restaurants, and a highlighted single-shop shortcut (e.g. d-mart) leads many to believe it's the only grocery option - so they never explore the full assortment and bounce when that shop lacks an item. Pandora is also pigeonholed as a solution for urgent, small needs, causing 37-45% to switch to competitors or physical stores for larger, planned weekly hauls; 32% of new users still prefer physical stores as more inspiring for discovery, and 45% value the social side of shopping. Cross-vertical awareness is low - only ~60% know Pandora offers non-food verticals.

delights.t: Reordering usuals makes restock effortless for QC users.
delights.w: Previous orders are the natural starting point for recurring grocery restock — users go straight from "what's missing" to a familiar basket, which is the low-effort backbone of the QC habit.

jtbd.functional: Restock what I need fast — heavy or urgent items — without a trip to the shop.
jtbd.emotional: Trust that groceries I can't physically inspect will still be fresh and good.
jtbd.social: Keep the household stocked with the brands and variety we rely on.

pains.t: QC users can't find everything they need in one place — assortment gaps push them to competitors.
pains.w: Assortment is the #1 retention barrier: the lack of variety, fresh produce and multi-vendor ordering drives over 50% of existing users to competitors or back to physical stores (especially APAC). Users switch because they can't find specialty foods (32%), household/cleaning supplies (29%), personal care (17%) or baby products (15%), and 36-47% cite the lack of multi-vendor ordering.

pains.t: A shop-first layout forces QC users to do the price comparison themselves.
pains.w: 76% of QC users know the items they want before opening the app, but the shop-first structure makes them browse store by store and mentally aggregate prices — extra work when building a multi-item basket, the same side-by-side comparison need seen across the platform.

quote.text: It's like for me it's another job to do... pick yogurt, and then whoever has the lower price then I choose.

pains.t: QC users can't judge product quality or value from the listing.
pains.w: Key grocery-decision details - size, weight, expiry, per-unit price, images, nutrition, authenticity - are missing or unclear, forcing "blind buys" or a retreat to familiar items. Trust in fresh produce is especially weak (new users rate it 4.0/7), and 20-26% of existing users are deterred by limited stock and the lack of visible freshness/expiry information. Users want reliable quality guarantees from Pandora itself - not just peer reviews, which feel low-value for everyday groceries - and worry about unreliable reviews and counterfeits in higher-stakes categories like Health & Beauty; nutrition and sustainability transparency is increasingly expected too.

pains.t: QC deals are hard to find and hard to understand.
pains.w: Offers like Mix & Match and Pro discounts are confusing, and incentives are scattered with unclear terms, so users struggle to tell what applies and how much they'll save while shopping.

delights.t: Finding familiar or unique products and brands delights QC users.
delights.w: Locating trusted staples or special/unique items is a bright spot - and users are genuinely surprised and delighted to discover specialty shops (pharmacy, deli, flowers, gifts) they didn't know Pandora offered, expanding their sense of what they can get.

delights.t: A valuable, relevant deal makes QC users feel they're shopping smart.
delights.w: Worthwhile discounts are a highlight of browsing groceries and help users feel they're getting real value — reinforcing the deal-driven reason many choose QC.

delights.t: Smart, personalised search delights QC users.
delights.w: Users feel understood when search remembers their behaviour - "Past Purchases" and favourites surfaced first - and when auto-suggestions cleanly narrow by sub-category and separate shops from restaurants; the prominent search bar makes starting easy.

jtbd.functional: Get the specific items I need, fast and at the best price — ideally all in one basket.
jtbd.emotional: Feel I'm getting a good deal without turning it into a chore.
jtbd.social: Keep the household stocked with what everyone needs.

jtbd.functional: Check out fast and pay reliably, seeing my real savings before I commit.
jtbd.emotional: Feel in control of a larger basket without fear of a bad total or failed payment.
jtbd.social: Stock up for the whole household in one confident checkout.

pains.t: Payment failures interrupt checkout for QC users.
pains.w: Account and payment issues at the point of paying disrupt QC orders - payment processing failures are the primary technical barrier, highest in Turkey (16%) - the same checkout failures seen across the app.

pains.t: Fees and minimums punish QC users for ordering across shops.
pains.w: Delivery fee, minimum order value and Pro benefits make multi-shop baskets uneconomical (12/12 sessions), and there's no multicart to shop several stores at once. New-to-QC users don't understand why they can't add items from different shops to one cart - it violates basic e-commerce expectations and leads to task abandonment - and users lose track of which store they're in.

pains.t: QC users struggle to confirm their real savings and apply the right voucher at the cart.
pains.w: Understanding total savings and comparing value in the cart is hard, coupons and discounts are unclear or inconsistent with earlier screens, and applying the best voucher takes manual effort — a moment where mismatched amounts drive abandonment.

delights.t: A clear cart-and-checkout flow makes finishing a QC order feel easy.
delights.w: The cart/checkout separation matches how users think and keeps a larger grocery basket manageable; saved carts and multicart are noticed and appreciated, and users generally find completing the order straightforward.

jtbd.functional: Know when my groceries will arrive so I can plan around them.
jtbd.emotional: Feel reassured my order is on track without having to keep checking.
jtbd.social: Time the delivery for when the household needs the items.

pains.t: QC users lose trust when delivery runs late with no real-time updates.
pains.w: Delays and unreliable delivery times are a key waiting-stage frustration, made worse by a lack of real-time updates and notifications. Restock shoppers especially want to know in advance when an order will arrive, so they can plan around it.

delights.t: A live map and clear progress updates turn waiting into reassurance for QC users.
delights.w: When present, map and progress indicators (and notifications, when enabled) reassure users their order is on track and reduce anxious re-checking.

jtbd.functional: Receive everything I ordered, fresh, correct and well packed.
jtbd.emotional: Trust the quality I couldn't inspect, and be recovered quickly if it's wrong.
jtbd.social: Keep the household supplied with items everyone can rely on.

pains.t: Fresh produce arrives in poor condition, or items don't match what QC users ordered.
pains.w: Poor-quality fresh produce and item mismatches are top receiving-stage frustrations; a bad delivery reinforces the very quality distrust that keeps people from ordering groceries online in the first place.

pains.t: Careless packaging leaves QC users unsure everything even arrived.
pains.w: Fresh, frozen and fragile items are packed together, plastic feels excessive, and there's no easy way to verify the full order was delivered — undermining confidence at the moment of unpacking.

pains.t: When a QC order goes wrong, cancellations and slow support let QC users down.
pains.w: Grocery orders get cancelled for item unavailability and delays, and when users need help, resolution lags competitors (~12% behind, ~28% CSAT gap for QC on communication) while help-center forms often can't capture the specific problem (missing/mismatched items) — so a bad moment isn't recovered well.

delights.t: Thoughtful packaging — and the occasional surprise — makes a QC order feel cared for.
delights.w: On-time delivery, considerate packaging done right, and small marketing surprises in the bag are the moments that make the receiving experience feel positive.

pains.t: Delivery-only users don't see a reason to try Pickup.
pains.w: Adoption is blocked by real-world friction (traffic, parking), no clear incentive (Pro already makes delivery free, and Pickup minimums aren't cheaper) and a fear the experience will fail (cold food, waiting). Cross-region survey data confirms strong, immediate financial incentives (discounts, free items, cashback) are the single most compelling trigger for a first Pickup trial, and that delivery-only users routinely multi-home across apps with low platform loyalty.

quote.text: It doesn't save that much time or money... at this moment there's no incentive for me.

pains.t: The way into Pickup is hidden — new and light Pickup users miss it entirely.
pains.w: The Pickup entry point sits in a secondary horizontal scroll and is easily missed, while promotional banners are ignored as clutter (assumed high minimum spend), blocking a key path into Pickup (8/11).

quote.text: The pickup option was actually quite hard for me to find because I have to scroll... it's a little bit hidden.

jtbd.functional: Save time and money by slotting a food run into my existing routine — commute, lunch break — without going out of my way.
jtbd.emotional: Stay in control of quality and skip the awkwardness of ordering in person or a failed delivery.
jtbd.social: Get in and out on my own terms, without crowds or awkward interaction.

jtbd.functional: Quickly find a nearby, viable place and confirm the real, discounted price.
jtbd.emotional: Feel sure it's worth the trip before I commit to going.
jtbd.social: Pick something that works for whoever I'm collecting for.

pains.t: Pickup users have to judge which places are even viable themselves — distance, parking and rating aren't surfaced.
pains.w: Before price or food, Pickup users apply a hard viability gate (proximity under ~500m, easy parking, high rating), but the app doesn't surface these clearly, so they filter mentally and distrust the sorting (8/11).

quote.text: I will sort it by distance... those over 500m I won't consider actually.

pains.t: Broken discovery tools push Pickup users into tunnel vision.
pains.w: The map is outdated and low-value and filters feel weak, so Pickup users ignore most of the interface and rely only on Search or scanning for pink discount tags — going blind to relevant options (9/11).

quote.text: That map is really old... now it's only showing that it's an empty place.

pains.t: Pickup users browse defensively because they can't trust the price or the mode.
pains.w: Menu prices don't reliably show the discounted Pickup price and the app sometimes reverts to Delivery, so users treat high prices as a warning sign and add items to the cart just to verify the real total (7/11).

quote.text: Sometimes the price is not right because somehow it changed to delivery... So I just swap it to pickup.

delights.t: Reorder and 'Popular' shortcuts let Pickup users choose fast.
delights.w: Heavy and Pickup-only users lean on Reorder, and lighter users use Popular/Recommendations swimlanes, to cut straight to a confident choice.

delights.t: Authentic food photos build Pickup users' trust in Pandora.
delights.w: Users easily spot competitors' AI-generated food images and find them off-putting, which increases their trust in Pandora's more authentic imagery.

quote.text: 100% sure this is not going to be the meal.
quote.attribution: Pickup user, on a competitor's AI image

jtbd.functional: Lock in the best price and pay ahead so collection is instant.
jtbd.emotional: Feel confident I'm getting the best deal before I set off.
jtbd.social: Sort a quick solo grab on my own terms.

pains.t: Payment failures interrupt checkout for Pickup users.
pains.w: The shared checkout payment failures also hit Pickup orders at the point of payment.

pains.t: Confirming the real discounted total is hard work — so Pickup users price-check competitors and may abandon.
pains.w: Discounts don't auto-apply and vouchers must be hunted manually, so users use the cart as a calculator and build parallel carts in competitor apps to compare the final total — churning at the last second if Pandora is pricier (7/11).

quote.text: Sometimes the app can't show the price after discount... so I put the food in my cart just to see the low price.

delights.t: The app's suggested best voucher is a feature Pickup users trust.
delights.w: In the voucher step, the app-suggested best voucher is called out as a trusted, effort-saving help at checkout.

jtbd.functional: Know exactly when the order is ready and when to leave to collect it.
jtbd.emotional: Avoid wasting a trip or waiting around at the counter.
jtbd.social: Fit the pickup neatly into my routine and other commitments.

pains.t: Unreliable 'ready for collection' times are Pickup users' single biggest frustration.
pains.w: The readiness estimate is so inaccurate that users regularly wait 10–30 minutes at the counter, which erases Pickup's time-saving promise; many now arrive deliberately late or call ahead to check (9/11). This is the #1 pain in the study.

quote.text: The app shows 10 minutes, but actually the waiting time is 20 minutes... I need to wait in front of the shop.

jtbd.functional: Find the counter and collect my correct order fast, without queueing.
jtbd.emotional: Feel the trip was worth it — quick, smooth and respectful of my time.
jtbd.social: Get in and out on my own terms, without crowds or awkward interaction.

pains.t: Scheduled Pickup orders arrive cold — prepared hours too early.
pains.w: When users schedule for later, restaurants often miss the pre-order flag and prepare the food hours ahead, so users collect cold food — a failure that breaks the core Pickup promise at the moment of collection.
